You don't need systemd to restart your compose service... Just have the service set to restart always or unless stopped.

And if you're running in Windows or Mac it's easier than the OS option usually.

You can use systemd and docker compose together. A systemd service is a single config file that runs the commands you give it, including `docker-compose` commands. Everything else about your service is still orchestrated via docker, and you can still run commands against the running containers just like before.

A big win with very little effort is systemd starting your docker compose service on boot. You have your systemd config file set `ExecStart` to call your docker-compose command, throw the config file into your systemd folder, and tell systemd to enable it. Docker compose handles the rest.

for long-running services, I've never taken the time to learn something reliable like systemd. with Compose, I can see everything I need to know in one yml file and the commands to go with it. I also don't have to really understand any dependencies or their own configuration and can cleanly remove everything associated with that service with a few commands.

You can't really host email with dynamic DNS. At least not well. You need stable MX records, you need various other DNS records for SPF/DMARC/DKIM, and most of all you need an IP address with a positive reputation. If you go changing your MX record constantly, you're not going to be receiving email reliably, if at all.

It's fine for casual game servers for friends.

Dynamic DNS clients are a thing. I host a bunch of stuff on my domain, the only issues I have are related to having a local address when I'm at home. I don't host game servers much, but I hosted terraria (tshock) for few a few years.

People should read the parent post and stop spreading FUD about email. The only part that isn't easy is the IP requirement. If you don't have a fixed public IP, preferably v4, then self-hosting email is out of reach, but so is hosting other things like game servers. It's the main cost of self-hosting, and one that isn't big relative to all the benefits. Privacy is the biggest one I think, and so is the ability to create unlimited aliases, one for each company/website.

You'll know from bounced email and logs, which you should have monitoring setup on.

It's not trivial to run your own email stack, but it's not hard either. It's more tedious than anything. Once it's up and running, it's low-maintenance. And it's fairly trivial to avoid spam. I get vastly more spam in my Gmail than I do on my self-hosted domains.

The biggest challenge with self-hosted email is getting an IP address that's not blocked or carrying low reputation. Most VPS IPs from e.g. Digital Ocean, Linode, Hetzner, AWS, etc. are going to get blocked from Google (the strictest) and Yahoo, Hotmail/Live/MS, etc. Cloud providers often block incoming and outgoing mail ports, too. I have a Digital Ocean VPS and my account is old enough to be grandfathered into the old policy, which means my email ports aren't blocked. I used to have no trouble sending email anywhere from my VPS, until I downsized it and got stuck with an IP in a bad reputation CIDR. children.author: dspillett
children.text:
You don't need to do it manually - the DNS challenge works automatically as long as the machine doing the renewing can call out to something to update the DNS entry, and you can use the dns-alias option¹ if your main DNS provider isn't easy to automate this way (this also limits the opportunities for something going wrong with the automatic DNS updates for certs breaking your main DNS at the same time).

I'm interested in the new DNS-persist method² which will make this even easier, though with some obvious trade-offs, but despite the announcements in Feb/May suggesting it would be rolled out in Q2, I've heard nothing recently and we are now in Q4.

There are various ways to separate managing certs via regular ACME renews and the hosts that actually use the certificates, meaning that hosts which can never see or be touched by the outside network (except via whatever VPN you may use when away yourself) can have ACME certs instead of you setting up your own CA arrangement to serve them. One option if you don't mind all your services having one private key, is to get a wildcard cert on one host (a small server just answering the top level domain.tld for HTTPS based validation, or again one of the DNS options) and have your other services regularly refresh the certificate they use by reading it from there.

----

[1] Docs for acme.sh: https://github.com/acmesh-official/acme.sh/wiki/DNS-alias-mo... (other tools work just as well with it)

[2] https://letsencrypt.org/2026/02/18/dns-persist-01

Oh goodness, I would never make this thing into a NAS. It’s a compute node with bootable storage and a second SSD for temporary storage of transcodes, nothing more.

Speaking of transcodes, I haven’t had an issue with either unit despite both handling hardware transcoding on a semi-regular basis (one for Plex, one for Jellyfin). The system cranks through them pretty decently provided you’re doing one or two at a time, and I’ve had no heating issues with them jammed in a rack with my NAS and network kit. The hardest part was getting Intel’s proprietary drivers working for such a feature, and that was more a (lack of) skill issue on my end than anything else.

They are absolutely great except: - you need a beefier GPU for transcoding. It heats up fast under heavy load and most builds are fanless. - you start to have NAS requirements / +2 hard drives, RAID etc. There are a few chinese motherboards/minipc options now that do 6 SATAs or 4 NVMEs (via PCIE 3.0 x1) but you will be quickly constrained.

It is the perfect gateway drug setup though.

Shoutout to another happy N100 miniPC user! I have two myself from before the RAMpocalypse, with one doing standard Proxmox + VMs work in a similar vein to ESXi, and the other straight Debian + Docker for more container hands-on time. Just the perfect little homelab boxes at the perfect price point (~$180US) before things got insane.

My stack is currently a mix of usual end user services (Jellyfin, FreshRSS) and identity infra, and it chugs along brilliantly without issue. I’m fairly certain that I could leave it running to the heat death of the universe if I built lifecycle management into my backup scripts.

I think with the advent of agents, self-hosting has become a lot easier. For example, I self-host an XMPP server, and in the past there were error cases where you could spend days finding out what was wrong.

A few weeks ago, I had trouble with audio and video calls. Sometimes they worked; sometimes they did not. So I gave an agent access to my phone via ADB and access to the server logs, and within 30 minutes the problem was clear, and the fix was deployed.

Background: During the last migration, I forgot to enable STUN/TURN discovery, and therefore the client did not find it and could not connect when both were behind NATs. And you don't have to trust those agents blindly; you can use it as a learning opportunity and understand everything before you do anything or ask questions.
